title: Oisin in the Land of Youth

blocks.text: When Saint Patrick came to Ireland, so the story goes, he met a very old man, blind and wrinkled and weak. The old man said he was Oisin, the son of Fionn, the great captain of the Fianna. But the Fianna had lived hundreds of years before. "How can you have lived so long?" Saint Patrick asked him. And this is the story Oisin told.

One dewy morning, Oisin was out hunting with his father, Fionn, and the Fianna, beside the lake of Lough Lein. The trees and hedges were all in blossom, and the little birds were singing. The hounds were chasing the deer across the plain, when suddenly the hunters saw a rider galloping towards them from the west.

It was a young woman on a white horse. She wore a thin golden crown, and a long brown silk cloak covered with little red-gold stars. Her golden hair flowed down over her cloak, and her eyes were as blue and clear as drops of dew. Her white horse had four shoes of pure gold. Nobody had ever seen anyone so lovely.
"Who are you, princess?" asked Fionn. "And where have you come from?"

"I have come a long way," she said, "from far across the Western Sea. I am the daughter of the king of Tirnanoge, the Land of Youth, and my name is Niam of the Golden Hair. Many princes have asked to marry me, but I have never loved anyone until I heard about your son, Oisin, and how brave and gentle he is. It is for him I have come."
As soon as Oisin looked at her, he loved her too. He took her hand and told her she was the one he would choose above all the princesses in the world.

"Then come with me to Tirnanoge," said Niam. "It is the most beautiful country under the sun. The trees have fruit and blossoms and green leaves all at the same time, all year round. There is honey and gold and music and feasting every day. You will have a hundred horses and a hundred hounds. And nobody there ever grows old or dies. You will be young for ever, and I will be your wife."
"I will go with you," said Oisin.

When Fionn and the Fianna heard this, they gave three great cries of sorrow. Fionn took his son's hand. "Oh, my son," he said sadly, "I don't think I will ever see you again." Oisin promised to come back soon, and he truly believed he would. But he couldn't stop his tears as he kissed his father goodbye.

Then he jumped up onto the white horse behind Niam, and they galloped away to the west. When the horse's golden hooves touched the sea, it shook itself and neighed three times. Then it raced straight out over the waves, as fast as the shadow of a cloud on a windy day. They overtook the wind, and soon there was no land to be seen, only waves in front of them and waves behind.

They passed many wonderful things: islands and cities and shining white palaces. A little deer went leaping from wave to wave, with a white hound with red ears chasing after it. A girl rode past on a brown horse, holding a golden apple, and a young warrior in a yellow silk cloak galloped after her.
"What does all this mean?" asked Oisin.
"Never mind these things," said Niam. "They are nothing compared with what you will see in Tirnanoge."

On the way, they came to a splendid palace beside the sea. "This is the Land of Virtues," said Niam. "A cruel giant lives here. He has stolen a princess away from her home and keeps her prisoner, and no hero has ever been brave enough to fight him."
"Then I will fight him," said Oisin, "and set her free."

The princess welcomed them with tears in her eyes, and gave them food and drink. While they were eating, the giant came stamping up to the palace, huge and ugly, with a great iron club in his hand. As soon as he saw Oisin, he shouted out a challenge to fight.

Oisin had fought many battles in Ireland, against wild boars and enchanters and invaders. But he had never had such a hard fight as this one. They fought for three days and three nights, with no food or drink or sleep. At last Oisin looked at the two princesses, so frightened, and he thought of his father, and his courage blazed up. With one great rush he knocked the giant to the ground, and the giant never got up again.

The princesses gave three cries of joy. The rescued princess put healing herbs on Oisin's wounds, and soon he was well again. In the morning, she said goodbye to them with tears, for she was sorry to see them go, even though she was happy to be free.

Then Oisin and Niam rode on over the sea. A great storm came up, with wind and lightning and huge waves, but the white horse galloped straight on through it all. When the storm was over and the sun came out again, there, close by, was a country all green and full of flowers, with smooth plains and blue hills, bright lakes and waterfalls. And near the shore stood a palace covered all over in gold and jewels, blue and green and red and yellow.
"This is my country," said Niam. "This is Tirnanoge."

The king and queen came out to meet them, with a hundred warriors and a hundred maidens. "Welcome, brave Oisin," said the king. "A hundred thousand welcomes! You will be young for ever in this land, and my daughter will be your wife." And there was a feast that lasted ten days, and on the last day Oisin and Niam were married.

Oisin was very happy in the Land of Youth. It seemed to him that about three years went by. But then he began to long to see his father, Fionn, and all his old friends again. So he asked the king and Niam if he might go home to Ireland for a visit.

"You may go," said Niam, "though it makes me very sad, because I am afraid you will never come back to me. Ireland is not as it was when you left it. Your father and the Fianna are all gone. Now listen carefully to what I tell you. If you get down off the white horse, you will never come back to me. Again I tell you: if your feet touch the green grass of Ireland, you will never return to this land. And a third time I tell you, my husband: if you get down off the white horse, you will never see me again."
"I will not get down," Oisin promised. And he looked at her sad face, and cried. But still he wanted to go.

So he rode the white horse back over the sea to Ireland. But when he got there, he hardly knew the old places. Everything had changed. There was no sign of Fionn or the Fianna anywhere. Then he met some people on horses. They looked very small to him, and they stared at Oisin in wonder, because to them he seemed like a giant.
"Where is Fionn?" he asked. "Where are the Fianna?"

"We have heard of Fionn," they said. "There are many old stories about him. But he and his Fianna lived long, long ago. We have read in old books that Fionn had a son called Oisin, who went away with a fairy princess to the Land of Youth, and was never seen again."
Then Oisin understood. Only three years had seemed to pass in Tirnanoge, but really it had been more than three hundred years.

With a heavy heart, he rode to his father's great house on the Hill of Allen. But the hill was empty and lonely, and the house was in ruins, all overgrown with grass and weeds. He searched all over Ireland, everywhere the Fianna used to live, but every place was the same: empty and ruined. Nobody knew him.

At last he came to a valley where he used to hunt in the old days. There he found a crowd of men trying to lift a big, flat stone. They had got it halfway up, but they weren't strong enough to lift it any further, and the men underneath were about to be crushed.
"Help us, mighty hero!" they cried.

Oisin leaned down from his horse, took hold of the stone with one hand, and threw it far away. The men were saved. But as he leaned over, the golden strap that held his saddle snapped. And to save himself from falling, Oisin jumped, and landed on the ground on his own two feet.

At once the white horse shook itself, neighed, and galloped away, as fast as a cloud's shadow, and Oisin was left standing alone. And in that very moment, all his three hundred years came upon him. His eyes grew dim, his strength drained away, and he fell to the ground, a poor, blind, wrinkled old man.
The white horse was never seen again. And Oisin lived on, old and blind, always missing his gentle, golden-haired wife, Niam, and thinking of his father, Fionn, and all the friends of his youth.

A simplified retelling of P. W. Joyce's “Oisin in Tirnanoge” in Old Celtic Romances (1879). The original is listed under Other versions. Joyce writes Niam for Niamh, and Tirnanoge for Tír na nÓg, the Land of Youth.
